title: Study notes
html:
Choose the tool by the question

Each technique sees one physical property: X-ray/CT see attenuation, US sees acoustic interfaces, MRI sees protons and their relaxation, nuclear medicine sees function (where a tracer goes). Ask what you want to know (anatomy, fluid, function, metabolism) and pick the technique that measures it.

Ultrasound

  • Piezo-electric probe emits and receives sound (2–15 MHz: higher = better resolution, less depth). Real-time, non-ionising, cheap, portable, repeatable, guides biopsies.
  • Limits: air (bowel gas, lung), bone, obesity, uncooperative patient, surgical dressings – and it is operator-dependent.
  • Doppler measures the frequency shift of echoes from moving blood: colour/power Doppler shows vessels without contrast; spectral Doppler gives velocities and resistive index.
  • Contrast US (CEUS): microbubbles – characterises liver lesions in real time, safe in renal failure.

Computed tomography

  • Rotating X-ray tube + detectors → axial slices, reconstructed in any plane; density in Hounsfield units (air −1000, fat −100, water 0, soft tissue 30–60, fresh blood 50–90, bone up to +1000).
  • Windows (soft tissue, lung, bone) only change display, not the data.
  • Phases: native (stones, calcification, blood, fat, adrenal HU) → arterial 25–35 s (hypervascular lesions, corticomedullary kidney) → portal 60–70 s (most staging, metastases) → nephrographic 90–100 s (renal masses) → excretory 5–10 min (urothelium = CT urography).
  • Dose rises with mAs, kV, number of phases, scan length; falls with higher pitch. Justify every phase.

MRI

  • Strong magnetic field aligns protons; an RF pulse excites them; they return RF signal while relaxing (T1 recovery, T2 decay). Source of information = radiofrequency waves, NOT X-rays.
  • T1: fat bright, fluid dark – anatomy, post-gadolinium. T2/STIR: fluid and oedema bright – pathology. Bright on T1: fat, subacute blood (methaemoglobin), melanin, protein, gadolinium.
  • Dark on everything: cortical bone, calcification, air, tendons, fast-flowing blood (flow void), metal.
  • Strengths: soft-tissue contrast, marrow, cartilage, ligaments, liver/pelvis/prostate/breast, no radiation. Limits: time, cost, claustrophobia, motion, unsafe implants, RF burns from bad positioning.
  • Liver-specific agents: gadoxetic acid (hepatobiliary phase: FNH stays bright, metastases/HCC dark; biliary leaks), SPIO (Kupffer cells).

Nuclear medicine

  • The source is inside the patient: radiopharmaceutical = isotope + vector. The gamma camera detects gamma rays leaving the body. Tc-99m: T½ 6 h, 140 keV, pure gamma emitter.
  • Bone scan (Tc-99m MDP/HMDP, images 2–4 h): whole skeleton in one exam, detects metastases months before X-ray (prostate, breast); myeloma often negative.
  • Renal: dynamic DTPA/MAG3 = split function, obstruction (furosemide), renovascular HT (captopril); static DMSA = cortical scars.
  • V/Q lung: perfusion Tc-99m MAA (lodges in pre-capillary arterioles); mismatch = embolism.
  • Parathyroid: Tc-99m MIBI. PET: FDG = glucose metabolism of viable tumour cells (staging, response, recurrence – not screening). Hybrids: SPECT/CT, PET/CT, PET/MRI.

Exam reflexes

  • US limits: obesity, air, uncooperative patient, scars – NOT sweating.
  • MRI: no ionising radiation; burns possible; slower than CT.
  • Scintigraphy irradiates the patient from inside – it is not a contrast agent, not an X-ray tube.
